quizzes.title: Module Intro: Before You Begin
quizzes.description:
MODULE INTRO
Module Intro: Before You Begin
3 questions · survey · one attempt
Instructions

Welcome to this module. This short survey is not graded for correctness. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting.

questions.text: After a great war, two strong nations that fought on the same side may become rivals. Why might that happen? Give your best answer now. You will come back to this question at the end of the module.

This module has these goals. Read them, then choose one answer.

  • Describe how the United States tried to build a lasting peace through the United Nations and Bretton Woods.
  • Explain how the Soviet Union came to control Eastern Europe.
  • Explain why Americans sent their soldiers home so quickly.
  • Describe the policy of containment and its first tests.
  • Explain the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, the Berlin Airlift, and NATO.
  • Weigh the arguments for and against containment.

answers.text: I have read the goals and I understand what this module asks of me.
I have read the goals, but I have a question about one of them.

questions.text: Some assignments in this course allow you to work with classmates. How do you plan to work this module?

answers.text: I would like to work with a group when that is an option.
I would rather work on my own.
I am not sure yet.

quizzes.title: Reading Quiz: Building the Postwar Order and Containment
quizzes.description:
READING QUIZ
Reading Quiz: Building the Postwar Order and Containment
8 questions · 8 points · one attempt
Before you start

Answer each question using what you learned in this week's two lessons. You may look back at them, but the answers are not stated word for word. You will need to put facts together.

questions.text: The United Nations Security Council gave each of five nations a permanent seat and a veto. Why did this design make it likely that the council would sometimes be unable to act?

answers.text: The General Assembly could overrule any decision of the council.
Any one of the five could block a decision, so when the great powers disagreed, nothing could be done.
The council had no power to order action to keep the peace.
Only members of the General Assembly were allowed to vote.

questions.text: The Senate approved the United Nations Charter by 89 to 2, though it had rejected the League of Nations in 1919. Which fact from the lesson best helps explain the difference?

answers.text: The United Nations had no power to act.
The Senate had changed its mind about Woodrow Wilson.
The Soviet Union had refused to join.
Roosevelt planned early and brought leading senators into the planning.

questions.text: The Bretton Woods Conference tied other currencies to the dollar and the dollar to gold. Which problem from the 1930s was this meant to prevent?

answers.text: Tariff wars and money troubles that choked trade.
A shortage of American soldiers.
The spread of communism in Asia.
The end of the Marshall Plan.

questions.text: At Yalta, Stalin promised "free and unfettered elections" in Poland. What does the lesson's account of Eastern Europe after 1945 suggest about that promise?

answers.text: It was kept in every country the Red Army entered.
It was kept in Poland but broken in Czechoslovakia.
It meant very little, since elections were rigged or put off and local communists took control.
It was canceled by a vote of the United Nations.

questions.text: Between 1945 and 1947, the armed forces shrank from about twelve million to fewer than two million. What was one result?

answers.text: The United States had far less force in Europe than the Soviet army, even though its factories were far larger.
The United States left Europe completely, as it had in 1919.
The Soviet Union demobilized at the same speed.
Congress ended the draft permanently.

questions.text: Kennan argued that Soviet leaders were cautious and would back away when they met firm resistance. Which action best fits a policy built on that belief?

answers.text: Pulling the American troops out of Berlin to avoid a clash.
Sending an armed convoy down the road into West Berlin to force it open.
Flying supplies into Berlin for months and holding the city without a shot.
Invading Eastern Europe to remove the communist governments.

questions.text: The Marshall Plan offered aid to all of Europe, yet Stalin forced the countries he controlled to refuse it. What was the effect?

answers.text: The plan failed everywhere in Europe.
Western Europe's economies stayed weak.
Communist parties gained ground in the West.
The aid went to Western Europe, where factories restarted and communist parties lost ground.

questions.text: Senator Robert Taft opposed the North Atlantic Treaty. Which concern did he hold?

answers.text: That the treaty cost too much money.
That it might drag the country into wars that Congress had not chosen.
That Britain and France could not be trusted.
That the Soviet Union would join NATO.

MODULE OUTRO
Module Outro: Looking Back

Instructions

You have finished this module. Please answer honestly. Your answers help your teacher see how the class is doing.

questions.text: Look back at the question from the start of the module. After a great war, two strong nations that fought on the same side may become rivals. Why might that happen? Give your answer now, using at least one fact from this module. You may say if your thinking has changed.
How confident do you feel about the material in this module?

answers.text: Very confident. I could explain it to someone else.
Fairly confident. I understand most of it.
Somewhat unsure. I understand parts of it.
Not confident. I need help.

questions.text: What is still unclear to you? Name a person, event, or idea. If nothing is unclear, write "nothing."
Which of these did the people in this module most need, whether they had it or not?

answers.text: Courage
Courtesy
Honesty
Perseverance
Self-government
Service
Responsibility

questions.text: Pick one person from this module (Truman, Kennan, Marshall, Stalin, Vandenberg, or someone else) and explain, in two or three sentences, how that virtue showed up in what they did, or how its absence did.

discussions.title: Discussion: Containment: Prudence or Provocation?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Discussion: Containment: Prudence or Provocation?
10 points · threaded discussion
Before you start

Open the lessons "Building the Postwar Order" and "Containment". Use My Notebook on those pages to gather your notes and marks, then come back here to post.

The question

After World War II, the United States chose a policy of containment: hold back the spread of Soviet power without going to war. Defenders call it a wise and careful choice. Critics say it turned a rivalry into a long confrontation. Was containment prudence, or provocation? Your job is to decide which view fits the evidence better.

Your post

Your post (about 100 to 150 words):

  1. Take a clear position: prudence, provocation, or a mix that leans one way.
  2. Give one specific piece of evidence from the lesson "Building the Postwar Order" or the source George Kennan, The Long Telegram that supports you.
  3. Name one fact that cuts against your position, and explain why you still hold it.
Your reply

Your reply (about 50 to 75 words): Respond to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with something they did not use. If not, say respectfully where their reasoning falls short.

Before you post

Post first, then reply. You will not see your classmates' posts until you have posted.

Rubric
Post and reply
10.0 pts		10.0 pts Substantive
Clear position, specific evidence from the week, names a counterpoint, and the reply engages a classmate's actual reasoning		6.0 pts Thin
Position stated but evidence vague, no counterpoint, or the reply only says "I agree"		0.0 pts Missing
No post, or no reply
